The need for a permitting reform package has only grown in the past decade, as bureaucracy has stymied the development of vital projects from clean energy to housing that could lower costs. And I appreciate the work done by Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich to negotiate a bipartisan agreement, as a lasting solution can only be reached by reaching across the aisle. In particular, the transmission and grid reform provisions are very positive. And the changes that they secured in the manager’s amendment make this a better bill. Nevertheless, the bill needs further improvement before I can support it.  

My top priorities in such an agreement are to bring down energy bills through new clean energy development, to lower emission rates, to support tribal sovereignty, and to stop the administration from attacking American clean energy projects. This includes restoring the billions of dollars in terminated energy projects in California, as well as the offshore wind projects the administration baselessly and illegally canceled. The president’s comments today, that notwithstanding any compromise in this bill, he intends to continue blocking wind projects, demonstrate a singular but telling lack of good faith. I have said from the start that we need to have confidence that any permitting reform legislation is not going to be weaponized by this or any future administration to single out states and provide giveaways to the oil and gas industries. In its current form, this bill does not satisfy those priorities and raises other serious concerns.  
  
This legislation would jeopardize tribal sovereignty through major changes to the National Historic Preservation Act, impact the State of California's authorities under the Clean Water Act, and constrict federal agencies’ ability to protect vulnerable wildlife under the Endangered Species Act. While I support the provisions in this bill that require data center companies to cover the costs of grid infrastructure and protect American taxpayers from footing the bill — which mirror my legislation — the legislation overall contains too many giveaways to oil and gas with insufficient constraints on an energy policy that has prioritized corporate profit over the pocketbooks of hard-working Americans and public health. I believe Congress should work on stronger guardrail provisions to ensure that such provisions will not be used to improperly tilt the playing field in favor of fossil fuels by the Trump administration, which has failed to provide any assurance to Congress that it will follow the law if this bill is enacted.

Throughout this trip, I heard over and over again how our interconnected commerce, markets and supply chains don't just impact our respective economies but also the livelihoods of Americans and Canadians alike.⁩⁩

No one on either side of the border thinks this tariff fight is a good idea. It’s hurt us all. That it has alienated one of our closest friends and allies adds additional salt to the wound. 

I will continue to do all I can to mitigate the impacts on Californians and our businesses until we can put an end to these tariffs.

I also met with the American Chamber of Commerce in Canada and representatives of American companies impacted by strained economic relations between our two countries.

Their stories mirror the many stories I've heard from California businesses about lost opportunities and how interconnected our commerce is with Canada.

I then traveled to Ottawa, the nation's capital, to sit down with Canadian Minister for Agriculture, Heath MacDonald, and members of Parliament to discuss these issues and what can be done to mitigate the harms to both our economies until we can end them. 

The tariff wars are raising costs in the United States on everything from steel and lumber to wine bottles to the potash farmers need for their fertilizer. Between the Canadian tariffs and the war in Iran (components of fertilizer also go through the Strait of Hormuz), the input costs for farmers have gone way up. 

Without American wine on Canadian shelves, Canadians are also missing out on tens of millions of dollars in tax revenue they would obtain from selling our wine.

My first stop was Alberta, the only province not boycotting Californian wines.

I spoke to provincial leaders about the importance of the Canadian market to California farmers and the importance of continuing close collaboration on dairy, beef and energy trade.

There is a political tradition in Canada, as there is in the United States, of politicians serving pancakes to their constituents. It was a pleasure to join Alberta’s Premier, Danielle Smith, for some good food and frank conversation about the needs of farmers in California and Alberta.

I just returned from my first CODEL to Canada, where I advocated for my California constituents suffering from the president’s tariff wars with our Northern neighbor.  

Canadians have been among our closest allies, fighting side-by-side in both world wars and innumerable other conflicts. 

When Los Angeles was burning, I met countless firefighters who came south to help us battle the blazes and save our homes and lives. 

Sadly, all too many Canadians feel betrayed by the President’s attacks on Canada, his demeaning comments about the country, and the 51st state nonsense. 

More to the point, the tariffs and a resulting Canadian boycott of certain American goods — like California wine — are hurting people on both sides of the border. 

And even if those trade disputes ended tomorrow, the damage will not disappear overnight. 
 
I went to understand more about how we can repair what is already broken, and the pathways to rebuilding an invaluable friendship with our neighbors.

Here’s what I saw:
Trump’s giving Kimberly Guilfoyle the Miranda Priestly treatment. https://t.co/AaN1M6e5NY

A filing lists assets, income, liabilities, and trades the member reported; it is not proof of a conflict or of wrongdoing. Dollar ranges and asset names are in the PDF. financial_disclosures.note: Senate financial disclosures are filed through efd.senate.gov, a different system from the House Clerk index used here. Senate filings are not listed yet.

conflicts.caption: These are overlaps in public records, not evidence of a deal. Lobbying can be for or against a bill, and donors' employers didn't necessarily give money.
conflicts.method: Each itemized donor dollar is counted once, under the industry of the donor's self-reported employer; an industry counts if at least one LD-2 client in it lobbied on any bill this member sponsored or voted on.

bills.vote_scope: Senate votes 1–262 of the 119th Congress, session 2 (262 votes, January 5, 2026 to November 12, 2026), from the Senate LIS.

overlap.cycle_note: Fallback cycle: these figures are from the 2024 two-year cycle (most recent completed election), not the current 2030 cycle. The 2030 cycle has no itemized donors yet.
